title: The two birds on one tree — one eats, one watches (3.1)
word: The two birds on one tree
hook: two birds share one tree: one pecks at the sweet figs, the other just watches, and the Mundaka says they're both you

segments.voice: Yesterday: the bow, the arrow and the target. Your line was tanmaya: like the arrow, become one with it. Did one task get the archer's full attention? Day four hundred seventeen.

Late at night, you're on your third episode, or your fourth cookie, or scrolling the same feed you just scrolled. And then, for a second, there's another part of you, a little above it all, noticing. Huh. Look at me. That part doesn't scold, exactly. It doesn't even stop you. It just sees. The Mundaka's third chapter opens with a picture of exactly that. It's older than the Upanishad itself. A tree, and two birds sitting in it.
screen: `THE THIRD EPISODE. THE FOURTH COOKIE.` → `A PART OF YOU, NOTICING.` → `A TREE, AND TWO BIRDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse. Dva suparna sayuja sakhaya. Two birds, close companions, always together, cling to the same tree. One of them eats the sweet fig. The other, not eating, looks on. The tree is the body, and the life lived in it. The bird that eats is the self as we usually know it, tasting every fruit, sweet ones and bitter ones, pleasure and pain, hungry for the next. The bird that watches doesn't eat at all. It isn't hungry. It just shines there, looking on. Then the next verse tells the story. On that same tree, the eating bird sinks down, confused, and grieves, feeling helpless. But when it sees the other, the Lord, content, and sees that one's greatness, its grief is gone. Notice: the eating bird doesn't have to fly to another tree. The watcher was on the same branch the whole time. This verse wasn't new when the Mundaka used it. It comes from the Rig Veda, from a hymn of riddles, and the Shvetashvatara Upanishad quotes it too. And here's where the schools of Vedanta part ways, honestly and for centuries. Advaita teachers read the two birds as one self seen two ways: the watcher is who the eater really is. Madhva's Dvaita school reads them as forever two, the soul and God, close companions who never merge. Ramanuja's school reads them as two, inseparably joined, the soul within God as a body within its self. All of them keep the comfort of the verse. The eater isn't alone. The watcher was always there.
screen: `TWO BIRDS, CLOSE COMPANIONS, ONE TREE.` · `ONE EATS THE SWEET FIG.` · `THE OTHER, NOT EATING, LOOKS ON.` · `SEEING THE WATCHER, GRIEF ENDS.` · then, large: `DVA SUPARNA.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with two birds. Sit, and let the eating bird be busy: thoughts, wants, a little itch, a plan for later. Let it peck. Now notice that something sees the pecking. It doesn't eat. It doesn't hurry. Rest with that one for a breath. When you get caught up in the pecking again, that's fine. Just look up, the way the eating bird looked up and saw its companion, still there on the same branch. The bell holds the time.
The two birds on one tree. In the Mundaka, one eats the sweet fruit and grieves; the other looks on, content; and seeing it, the first is freed from grief.
Your line: the one who watches. Today, in the middle of a craving or a scroll, look up, once, at the bird on the same branch. Day four hundred seventeen.

howItsDone: The two-birds verse is chanted in Vedic recitation and quoted by teachers of every Vedanta school, each of whom explains the relation between the two birds in its own way.

original.note: Sanskrit dvā suparṇā, two birds (literally, two of fine wings): Mundaka 3.1.1, from Rig Veda 1.164.20.

trapdoor: what you thought: the watching bird is your conscience, scolding you.
what it means: one bird tastes life's fruit and grieves; the other, content, looks on; seeing it ends the grief.
what a scholar hears: Rig Veda 1.164.20, from the riddle hymn ascribed to Dirghatamas; reused in Mundaka 3.1.1 and Shvetashvatara 4.6.

sources.ref: Mundaka Upanishad 3.1.2 (the eating bird grieves; seeing the Lord, freed from grief)

notes: 'The tree is the body' is the commentators' reading (e.g. Shankara), not stated in 3.1.1 itself; the script presents it as the reading. Confirm phrasing.
Rig Veda 1.164 attributed to Dirghatamas by tradition; confirm.
